meta.title: Hindi B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hindi → English (see the Hindi, recall the meaning) and English → Hindi (see an English meaning, recall the Hindi). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hindi, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 177 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work, money and the economy, education, the news, media and technology, government, law and society, the environment and the weather, health and medicine, travel and transport, the household and its chores, relationships and the stages of life, feelings and character, religion and festivals, abstract nouns for ideas, reasons and plans, the connectors that join sentences, and the verbs of thinking, deciding, arguing and changing — and the other 823 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Hindi, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in Devanagari with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ā ī ū for the long vowels, a tilde or a dot for nasalisation: khānā, ma͠i), so the deck can be studied before the script is fluent; the Hindi Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. The 660 nouns show their gender, masculine or feminine, which every adjective, postposition and past-tense verb agrees with, and their plural; the 77 verbs show their past forms, where Hindi verbs are irregular, and behind the All forms fold their present, future, subjunctive and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 578 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 285 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
